questions.question_text:
A radio station wants to find local residents’ views about lowering a highway speed limit. It invites listeners to phone in and reports the views of the $720$ listeners who choose to call.
Why may the sample be unrepresentative?

options.text: Only listeners who choose to call are included, and their views may differ from those of other residents
The callers are chosen randomly because the station cannot predict who will call
options.why: Confuses unpredictable voluntary replies with random selection from all local residents.

options.text: Having $720$ replies guarantees that all local views are represented
options.why: Assumes a large number of replies removes the exclusion of non-listeners and people who do not volunteer.

options.text: Everyone hears the same invitation, so everyone has the same chance of being included
options.why: Assumes all residents hear the station and ignores that inclusion depends on choosing to call.

questions.solution_text:
The population is all local residents.
The sample includes only listeners who hear the invitation and choose to call.
Non-listeners and people who do not call are left out, and their views may differ from those of callers.
**The sample risks selection bias and volunteer bias**.

questions.question_text:
A phone-repair chain tests $3$ of the $900$ replacement screens it received in a delivery, finds no fault in any of them, and reports that the delivery is free of faults.
What is the main weakness of this study?

options.text: Three screens are far too few to show how common a fault is in $900$
The screens should have been chosen by the supplier rather than the chain
options.why: Hands selection to the party with an interest in a clean result, which weakens the study further.

options.text: Testing screens destroys them, so no screen should have been tested
options.why: Nothing in the question says that testing destroys a screen. Even if a test were destructive, that would not mean no sample could be tested.

options.text: All $900$ screens can be assumed to be fault-free because these three passed
options.why: A test of three screens does not establish that the other $897$ screens are fault-free.

questions.solution_text:
Only $3$ of the $900$ screens were tested. Faults among the other $897$ screens may have been missed. A few successful tests do not show that the whole delivery is fault-free.
**Three screens are far too few to show how common a fault is in $900$**.

questions.question_text:
A university wants to know how its $25\,000$ students rate campus parking. An open poll on its student website receives $5200$ voluntary responses.
The university claims that the result represents all students because so many answered.
Which statement best explains why this claim may not be valid?

options.text: Students who choose to answer may have different views from those who do not, so many replies do not remove volunteer bias
The claim is valid because $5200$ responses is a large sample
options.why: Treats sample size as proof of representativeness and ignores how respondents entered the sample.

options.text: The claim is valid because every student was required to answer
options.why: Replaces the stated voluntary participation with a requirement that the question does not give.

options.text: The result is invalid simply because fewer than all $25\,000$ students answered
options.why: Assumes every sample is invalid; the concern here is voluntary selection and possible differences between respondents and non-respondents.

questions.solution_text:
The population is all $25\,000$ students.
Only the $5200$ students who choose to answer the website poll are included.
$25\,000-5200=19\,800$ students do not answer.
Students with strong opinions about parking may be more likely to reply, while students who do not use the website or do not volunteer are missing.
**The claim may not be valid because of volunteer bias and possible selection bias**.
The number of replies does not establish the views of non-respondents.
